title: 22. Interview: Design Twitter / X
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Twitter / X — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Twitter / X interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read (hybrid)**: write-time work vs read-time latency. Hybrid threshold of 100 k followers is the sweet spot Twitter reportedly uses.
- **Cassandra vs MySQL for tweets**: LSM-tree writes + automatic sharding (Cassandra) vs mature ACID (MySQL). Twitter chose Cassandra in 2010 after MySQL replication broke at scale.
- **Snowflake vs auto-increment vs UUID**: monotonic + sortable (Snowflake) vs sequential (auto-increment, single point of failure) vs random (UUID, no time order).
- **Redis list vs Cassandra pre-materialized timeline**: ~1 ms reads + small write cost (Redis) vs durable but slower (Cassandra). Use Redis as L3, Cassandra as fallback.
- **Trending bucketed vs exact sliding window**: bucketed (approximate, O(1) per hashtag) vs exact (O(N) per request, requires keeping every event).

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why does Twitter use a hybrid fanout (write for normal users, read for celebs) instead of pure fanout-on-write?
**Answer:** Pure fanout-on-write gives O(1) timeline reads — perfect for normal users, where 100 followers × 5 800 tweets/s = 580 k Redis LPUSHes/s is manageable. But a celebrity with 100 M followers would generate 100 M Redis writes per tweet, multiplying the platform's total write load by 100–1000× for just a few hundred celeb accounts. Worse, most of those writes go to inactive users who never read them, wasting Redis memory and CPU. By switching to fanout-on-read for celebs (pull their recent tweets at read time, merge with cached feed), we cap the worst-case write fanout at ~100 k per tweet while adding only ~10 ms of read latency for the small fraction of a user's follows who are celebs (typically < 1 % of follows). The 100 k threshold is empirically tuned: below it, the write cost is acceptable; above it, the wasted-work cost dominates.
**Visual:**
```
Normal user (50 followers):                Celeb (100M followers):
  tweet -> 50 LPUSHes (~5ms)                 tweet -> SKIP fanout
  read  -> LRANGE feed (~1ms)                read  -> pull 10 recent from user_tweets
                                                  + merge with cached feed
                                                  +10ms latency, 100M writes saved
```

### Q2. How does Snowflake guarantee globally unique, time-sortable IDs without a central coordinator?
**Answer:** Snowflake splits the 64-bit ID into three fields: 41 bits of millisecond timestamp (since a fixed epoch, ~69 years of range), 10 bits of machine/worker ID (1 024 workers), and 12 bits of per-millisecond sequence (4 096 IDs per ms per worker). Each worker is assigned a unique `machine_id` at startup (via ZooKeeper / etcd lease), so two workers never collide on the `machine_id` field. Within one worker, the sequence counter resets to 0 each millisecond and increments for each ID — if it overflows (4 096 IDs in 1 ms on one worker), the generator blocks until the clock advances. This gives 4 096 × 1 024 = ~4 M IDs per ms globally, with no central coordinator after worker assignment. Because the timestamp is the high bits, IDs are sortable by time — `ORDER BY id DESC` == `ORDER BY created_at DESC`, which lets us paginate timelines by `WHERE id < ?` without a separate cursor column. Twitter open-sourced this in 2010; Instagram, Discord, and many others use the same pattern.
**Visual:**
```
| 41 bits timestamp (ms since epoch) | 10 bits machine | 12 bits seq |
| <------- ~69 years of range -----> | <-- 1024 wrks ->| <-4096/ms-> |
```

### Q3. Why did Twitter migrate tweet storage from MySQL to Cassandra in 2010?
**Answer:** Twitter's MySQL deployment had reached its limit: tweets grew 5 800/s sustained with 100× spikes during live events, and MySQL's master-slave replication couldn't keep up — replicas lagged by minutes, write contention on the master forced manual sharding, and operations required constant babysitting (manual sharding, failovers, schema migrations). Cassandra, by contrast, offers: (1) masterless peer-to-peer replication — any node accepts writes, no single bottleneck; (2) LSM-tree storage engine that handles write-heavy workloads orders of magnitude better than MySQL's B-tree; (3) automatic sharding via consistent hashing — add a node, the ring rebalances without operator intervention; (4) tunable consistency — LOCAL_QUORUM for strong-enough reads, ANY for fire-and-forget writes; (5) linear horizontal scalability. Twitter reported a 4× write throughput improvement and dramatically reduced operational burden after migration. The trade-off: Cassandra's data model is less flexible than SQL (no JOINs, denormalized tables), and counters are eventually consistent — but for tweets, those trade-offs were acceptable.
**Visual:**
```
MySQL (2006-2010):                Cassandra (2010+):
+------+                          +----+ +----+ +----+
|master|--replicate-->slave1      | N1 |<->| N2 |<->| N3 |  (ring)
+------+              slave2      +----+ +----+ +----+
   ^                                  ^ LSM-tree writes
   | bottleneck: single writer        ^ auto-shard via consistent hash
   | manual sharding                  ^ no master
```

### Q4. How would you implement trending topics, and why is a naive "COUNT per hashtag in last 24 h" not enough?
**Answer:** A naive `SELECT hashtag, COUNT(*) FROM tweets WHERE ts > now()-24h GROUP BY hashtag` would require scanning billions of rows per query — totally infeasible. Instead: (1) Every tweet emits a `(hashtag, region, ts)` event to a `hashtags` Kafka topic. (2) A Flink streaming job maintains bucketed counters: divide time into 1-minute buckets, keep the last 1 440 buckets (= 24 h) per hashtag per region in Redis as a sorted set with score = count. (3) Top-N is just `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE trending:{region}:{window}`. (4) To handle spam: only count hashtags from accounts > 30 days old, dedupe by device fingerprint per hashtag, apply a minimum-volume threshold (e.g., 1 000 mentions in window) and an anomaly detector for velocity (3× normal in 1 min → flag). (5) Smooth the top-N: filter hashtags that flash for 1 minute then vanish by requiring sustained presence across 3 consecutive buckets. Twitter's actual algorithm is similar, with additional ML-based "trend type" classification (news, sports, entertainment).
**Visual:**
```
tweets -> Kafka(hashtags) -> Flink -> Redis bucketed counters
                                          |
  bucket 14:23: hashtag=coffee score=1234 |
  bucket 14:24: hashtag=coffee score=1456 |
  ...                                     v
  bucket 14:22 next day (rolling expiry)  ZREVRANGE trending:US:24h 0 9
```

### Q5. How do you handle the read-after-write problem — when a user posts a tweet and immediately refreshes their timeline?
**Answer:** Without special handling, there's a race: the tweet is written to Cassandra (fast), but the fanout worker hasn't yet LPUSHed it to the author's `feed:{author_id}` (Kafka lag + worker processing = 100 ms–2 s latency). The user refreshes, sees no new tweet, and thinks the post failed — a frustrating UX. Two fixes: (1) **Eager self-fanout**: the Tweet Service, after writing to Cassandra, immediately LPUSHes the tweet ID into `feed:{author_id}` before returning 200 OK to the client. The Kafka-driven fanout still runs for the author's followers, but the author's own timeline is updated synchronously. (2) **Client-side dedup**: the client includes the just-posted tweet ID in the next `GET /timeline/home` request as a `?since_id=` parameter; if the server's response doesn't include it (because fanout hasn't run), the client prepends it locally. Twitter uses approach (1) — guaranteed self-visibility at the cost of one extra Redis write per tweet (negligible).
**Visual:**
```
Client posts tweet
   |
   v
Tweet Service:
   1. INSERT into Cassandra.tweets      (~5ms)
   2. LPUSH feed:{author} tweet_id       (~1ms)  <-- eager self-fanout
   3. publish Kafka tweet-created        (~1ms)
   4. return 200 OK {tweet_id}           (total < 10ms)
   |
   v (later, async)
Fanout Worker -> LPUSH feed:{follower1}, feed:{follower2}, ...
```

### Q6. How do you implement "Edit Tweet" (X's 2022 feature) without breaking timelines and replies?
**Answer:** Edits are versioned, not in-place updates — preserving the original text for legal/historical reasons (replies may quote the original). Schema: `tweets` table keeps `current_version`, `edit_window_expires_at`; a new `tweet_versions(tweet_id, version, text, edited_at)` table stores each version. Constraints (X's actual policy): only editable within 30 min of posting, only by the original author, max 5 edits. Read path: Timeline Service hydrates `tweets.current_version` joined with `tweet_versions.text`. Reply chain: replies still reference the original `tweet_id`; the parent tweet's display may show "Edited" badge. Cache invalidation: since the timeline cache stores only `tweet_id` (not the text), an edit invalidates only the per-tweet object cache (one Redis `DEL tweet_obj:{id}`), not the feed lists — so the next hydrate picks up the new text automatically. Trade-off: versioning increases storage by ~10 % for editable tweets, but the alternative (in-place mutation) breaks audit trails and quoted tweets.
**Visual:**
```
tweets: {tweet_id=42, current_version=3, edit_window_expires_at=14:30}
tweet_versions:
  (42, 1, "original text",     14:00)
  (42, 2, "fixed typo",        14:05)
  (42, 3, "final wording",     14:10)   <-- current
Timeline reads: tweets.current_version=3 -> tweet_versions(42,3)
```

### Q7. How would you design Tweet Storms (threads) so they display as a single expandable unit?
**Answer:** A thread is N tweets posted by the same author in sequence, each replying to the previous. The simplest implementation: client calls `POST /tweets` N times with `reply_to` = previous tweet's ID. But this is slow (N round-trips) and non-atomic (partial threads on failure). Better: a dedicated `POST /tweetstorm` endpoint that takes a list of tweet bodies, opens a transaction, allocates N Snowflake IDs, sets each tweet's `reply_to` to the previous ID, tags all with a shared `thread_id` (another Snowflake), writes them all to Cassandra in a batch, publishes one Kafka event with the whole thread. Read path: when Timeline Service encounters a tweet with `thread_id != null`, it can optionally fetch the full thread via `SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE thread_id = ? ORDER BY tweet_id` and render it with "Show this thread" affordance. Fanout: a single fanout-on-write per tweet in the thread (each tweet is a separate timeline entry), but the client renders them grouped. Trade-off: storing `thread_id` adds one column; the alternative (chain via `reply_to` only) requires N recursive queries to reconstruct the thread.
**Visual:**
```
POST /tweetstorm {tweets: ["1/ Intro", "2/ Detail", "3/ Conclusion"]}
    |
    v
Tweet Service (atomic batch):
  tweet_id=100, thread_id=99, reply_to=null,    text="1/ Intro"
  tweet_id=101, thread_id=99, reply_to=100,     text="2/ Detail"
  tweet_id=102, thread_id=99, reply_to=101,     text="3/ Conclusion"
    |
    v
Timeline renders: "1/ Intro  [Show this thread -> 2/ Detail, 3/ Conclusion]"
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A celebrity with 50 M followers tweets during the Super Bowl. The fanout worker's Kafka lag grows to 5 minutes. How do you prevent timelines from being stale?
**Answer:** First, this is exactly the case the hybrid fanout was designed for — the celebrity's tweet was skipped during fanout-on-write, so there's no Kafka backlog caused by them. The lag is from other normal-user tweets during the spike. Three-layer mitigation: (1) **Auto-scale fanout workers** based on Kafka consumer lag — spin up 3× workers within 2 minutes via Kubernetes HPA on a custom lag metric. (2) **Prioritize freshness over completeness**: when lag > 30 s, the Fanout Worker switches to a "burst mode" that processes only tweets from the last 60 s, dropping older events to a dead-letter queue for later backfill. (3) **On-read fallback**: Timeline Service detects when `feed:{user_id}` hasn't been updated recently (LRANGE returns timestamps older than 1 min) and falls back to pulling recent tweets from `user_tweets` of all follows directly — slower (p99 ~500 ms vs 200 ms) but fresh. For the celeb tweet specifically, it was always pulled on-read, so it appears instantly for any user who follows the celeb. Post-event: drain the dead-letter queue, verify no permanent loss (Snowflake IDs make dedup trivial), and update the auto-scaling threshold for next time.
**Visual:**
```
Super Bowl spike:
  tweets/s: 5,800 -> 50,000 (10x)
  Kafka lag: 5 min

Worker autoscaler (HPA on lag metric):
  workers: 100 -> 300 in 2 min
  lag drops: 5min -> 30s

Timeline Service fallback:
  if (feed age > 60s):
     pull user_tweets for all follows  (slower but fresh)
```

### Q2. A coordinated botnet creates 100 k fake accounts and tries to push a hashtag to trending. How do you detect and prevent it?
**Answer:** Multi-layer defense: (1) **Account age gate**: only count hashtags from accounts > 30 days old — botnet accounts are typically new. This alone blocks ~80 % of attacks. (2) **Device fingerprint dedup**: each hashtag-event includes a device fingerprint (IP + UA + app install ID). Within a 5-min window, the same fingerprint can contribute at most 3 mentions to a single hashtag. (3) **Velocity anomaly**: maintain a baseline of normal hashtag velocity per region per hour. If a hashtag's 5-min velocity is > 3× its 24-h baseline, flag it for manual review or auto-demote in trending. (4) **Network graph analysis**: build a graph of accounts that all tweeted the same hashtag within a short window. If a connected cluster of > 1 000 accounts has high edge density (all follow each other, all created within a week), it's almost certainly coordinated — exclude their contributions. (5) **CAPTCHA / phone verification**: if a hashtag is flagged, require accounts < 30 days old that want to contribute to pass a CAPTCHA or SMS verification. (6) **Manual review queue**: the top 100 trending candidates per region pass through a human reviewer within 5 min before being displayed prominently. Twitter's actual anti-manipulation system uses similar layered defenses and reportedly catches > 90 % of botnet attempts.
**Visual:**
```
Hashtag events -> [Age gate >30d] -> [FP dedup ≤3/5min]
                                          |
                                          v
                                     [Velocity anomaly >3x baseline]
                                          |
                                          v
                                     [Network graph: dense cluster?]
                                          |
                                          v
                                     [Human review queue] -> Trending
```

### Q3. A user deletes a tweet that has been retweeted 1 M times. What happens to the retweets?
**Answer:** This is a soft-delete problem with cascading implications. The design: (1) **Soft-delete the original**: `UPDATE tweets SET deleted_at = now() WHERE tweet_id = ?`. The row stays in Cassandra for 30 days (for appeal / legal / analytics), then is hard-deleted by a TTL compaction. (2) **Retweets are references, not copies**: the `retweets` table stores `(retweet_id, original_tweet_id, user_id, ts)`. When Timeline Service hydrates a retweet, it joins to `tweets` — if the original has `deleted_at != null`, the timeline entry is suppressed (or rendered as "This tweet was deleted"). (3) **Cache invalidation**: the deleted tweet's `tweet_obj:{id}` cache entry is `DEL`eted. The feed lists (which contain retweet IDs, not original tweet IDs) are not invalidated — the next hydrate will fetch the original and see it's deleted. (4) **Quoted tweets**: a quote tweet has its own text, so it can still be displayed with "The quoted tweet was deleted" placeholder. (5) **Replies to the deleted tweet**: stay visible (they're separate tweet rows), but the parent reference is shown as deleted. (6) **Reposts / screenshots off-platform**: nothing we can do — that's a content moderation / legal issue, not an architecture one. The whole design hinges on retweets being references rather than copies — which is why Twitter stores them as `(original_tweet_id, retweeter_id)` rather than duplicating the content.
**Visual:**
```
Original tweet T1 (deleted at 14:30)
  |
  +-- retweet R1 (by Alice)   -> hydrate: T1.deleted_at!=null -> suppress
  +-- retweet R2 (by Bob)     -> hydrate: T1.deleted_at!=null -> suppress
  +-- quote tweet Q1 (by Carol, with Carol's own text) -> show "Quoted tweet deleted"
  +-- reply P1 (by Dan, "great point") -> stay visible, parent shown as deleted
```

### Q4. Your Cassandra cluster is experiencing hot partitions during a viral event — one user's `user_tweets` partition is getting 100× the normal write rate. How do you mitigate?
**Answer:** This happens when a single user posts dozens of tweets per minute during a viral moment (e.g., live-tweeting the Oscars). All writes hit the same `user_tweets` partition (keyed by `user_id`), overwhelming one Cassandra node. Mitigations in order: (1) **Identify the hot partition**: Cassandra's `TableHistograms` MBean shows partition size skew. Set up an alert on partition write rate ratio (max/median > 10×). (2) **Time-bucket the partition**: change `user_tweets` primary key from `(user_id, created_at)` to `((user_id, date_bucket), created_at)` where `date_bucket = created_at / 86400s`. This splits one user's writes across daily sub-partitions — a single user can now write up to N× the per-node rate before becoming hot. (3) **Throttle the user**: API gateway enforces a tighter per-user rate limit (e.g., 50 tweets/hour) — viral live-tweeting should be paced, not banned. (4) **Read-side caching**: cache the user's recent tweets in Redis `user_tweets:{user_id}` so reads don't hit the hot Cassandra partition. (5) **Last resort: vnodes**: increase the cluster's vnode count from 256 to 512 per node, which spreads partitions more uniformly and reduces the chance of one hot partition landing on a single node. Twitter actually faced this in 2014 with live-tweeting of the Oscars and adopted time-bucketed partitions as a fix.
**Visual:**
```
Before: user_tweets PK = (user_id, created_at)
  viral user U1 -> ALL writes hit partition (U1) on node N7
  N7 CPU = 95%, other nodes = 10%

After:  user_tweets PK = ((user_id, date_bucket), created_at)
  viral user U1 day-1 writes -> partition (U1, 20240115) on N3
  viral user U1 day-2 writes -> partition (U1, 20240116) on N11
  Hot load spread across nodes by date
```

### Q5. Your trending service shows a hashtag that's actually a typo of a real trend (e.g., #Brexit vs #Brexut). How do you handle typo trends?
**Answer:** Typos and misspellings of major trends are common — they fragment the signal and create user confusion. Three approaches: (1) **Spell correction at index time**: maintain a dictionary of "verified" trends (manually curated + machine-learned from past trending). When a new hashtag hits a velocity threshold, run edit-distance (Levenshtein) against the verified dictionary; if distance ≤ 2 to a verified trend with > 10× the volume, alias the typo to the canonical. (2) **Co-occurrence clustering**: if users who tweet #Brexut also frequently tweet #Brexit in the same session, that's strong evidence they meant the latter — merge them. (3) **User-facing merge**: in the trending UI, show "#Brexut" but redirect clicks to "#Brexit | #Brexut" combined view, with a tooltip "Did you mean #Brexit?". (4) **Suggestion at compose time**: when a user types #Brexut in the composer, show a dropdown "Did you mean #Brexit (1.2 M tweets)?" — preventing the typo from being created in the first place. (5) **Manual override**: a human reviewer can merge typo trends into canonical ones via an admin tool. Trade-off: aggressive merging can suppress legitimate new trends (a new meme that happens to be one edit-distance from a known one). Always log merges for audit.
**Visual:**
```
Hashtag stream:
  #Brexit  (1,200,000 tweets)
  #Brexut  (   45,000 tweets)   <-- edit distance 1 from #Brexit

Auto-merge logic:
  if (Levenshtein(typo, canonical) <= 2 AND volume(typo) < 0.1*volume(canon)):
      alias(typo -> canonical)

Trending UI:
  #Brexit  1.245M tweets  (includes #Brexut)
```

### Q6. The CEO wants a "Close Friends" feature (like Instagram's) — sharing tweets with a subset of followers. How do you extend the design?
**Answer:** The challenge is access control at scale: a "Close Friends" tweet must be visible to ~20 selected followers but hidden from the user's other 5 000 followers. The current fanout-on-write pushes to all followers' feeds — that won't work. Design: (1) **New tweet visibility field**: `tweets.visibility IN ('public', 'followers', 'close_friends')`. (2) **Close friends list**: stored in Postgres `close_friends (user_id, friend_id)`, cached in Redis `cf:{user_id}` as a set. (3) **Fanout change**: for `close_friends` tweets, the Fanout Worker fetches the close friends list (not the full followers list) and LPUSHes only to those ~20 feeds. (4) **Read-time enforcement**: even with fanout, a malicious user could try to fetch the tweet directly via `GET /tweets/{id}`. Timeline Service checks `visibility` and `cf:{poster_id} ∋ reader_id` before returning the tweet object; if denied, returns 403. (5) **Cache hygiene**: the per-tweet object cache stores the visibility level; on close-friends list change, the relevant tweets' caches are invalidated. (6) **Search exclusion**: close-friends tweets are excluded from Elasticsearch index entirely (no public search). (7) **CDN auth**: media assets get signed URLs with short TTLs (5 min) so a leaked URL doesn't grant permanent access. Trade-off: this adds 2 Redis lookups per tweet hydrate (visibility + membership), roughly doubling the hydrate cost. We can amortize by batching — fetch visibility for 20 tweet IDs in one MGET, and check membership for the user's entire close-friends set once per request.
**Visual:**
```
Poster P posts close-friends tweet T:
  Fanout Worker:
    cf_list = SMEMBERS cf:P           # {Alice, Bob, Carol}
    LPUSH feed:Alice T
    LPUSH feed:Bob   T
    LPUSH feed:Carol T
    (skip 5,000 other followers)

GET /tweets/T by Eve (not in cf:P):
  Timeline Service:
    if T.visibility == 'close_friends' AND Eve not in cf:P:
        return 403 Forbidden
```

### Q7. During a regional outage (us-east-1 goes down), how does Twitter stay available globally?
**Answer:** Twitter's design is multi-region active-active: two AWS regions (e.g., us-east-1 + eu-west-1) each run the full stack, with Cassandra configured for multi-DC replication (NetworkTopologyStrategy, RF=3 per DC, LOCAL_QUORUM for reads/writes). When us-east-1 fails: (1) **Route 53 health checks** detect the failure within 30 s and shift DNS traffic for `api.twitter.com` to eu-west-1. (2) **Cassandra continuity**: eu-west-1 already has a full copy of tweets (replicated async with ~1 s lag). New tweets written to eu-west-1 replicate back to us-east-1 when it recovers. (3) **Redis failover**: each region has its own Redis cluster with its own feed cache; users routed to eu-west-1 will have a "cold" feed cache initially (cache miss → Cassandra fallback → repopulate). This means the first ~1 min of reads in the failover region are slower (p99 ~500 ms vs 200 ms). (4) **Kafka MirrorMaker**: the `tweet-created` topic is mirrored between regions, so fanout workers in eu-west-1 process tweets originally published in us-east-1 (and vice versa). (5) **User-facing impact**: ~30 s of 5xx errors during DNS failover, then ~1 min of slower-than-normal reads as caches warm. No data loss because Cassandra writes were LOCAL_QUORUM in the surviving region. (6) **Failback**: when us-east-1 recovers, Cassandra hints (Hinted Handoff) replay missed writes, and traffic is gradually shifted back via weighted DNS (10 % → 50 % → 100 %) over 30 min to avoid thundering-herd. Netflix's Chaos Kong drills (which intentionally take down entire regions) validate this pattern; Twitter has run similar drills since 2013.
**Visual:**
```
Normal:                         us-east-1 outage:
+--------+    +--------+        +--------+    +--------+
|us-east1|<-->|eu-west1|        |us-east1|    |eu-west1|
|active  |    |active  |        | DOWN   |    |active  |
+--------+    +--------+        +--------+    +--------+
    ^                              |               ^
    | 50% traffic                  |               | 100% traffic
    v                              v               v
Route 53 health check -> 30s detect -> DNS failover -> eu-west1
                                                       (cache cold for ~1 min)
```
